title: Five friends in a deer park

hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? when something hurts, what do you want first?
options: then you’ll like this teacher. listen.
To know how to fix it
then you’ll like him too. listen.
i’m here. and this story begins with old friends.

steps.line: After he woke up under the Bodhi tree, the Buddha walked a long way to a deer park near Varanasi, to find five old friends.
Years before, these five had stayed by his side through his hardest fasting. When he chose to eat again, they walked away from him.
Now they saw him coming. “Here comes Gotama, who gave up the striving,” they said. “We won’t stand. We won’t greet him.”

steps.q: They’ve agreed to snub him. What happens as he walks up?
o: They keep their word and look away
They get up and leave the park
They can’t help it, and rise to welcome him
steps.why: Something about him had changed. Their plan fell apart.

steps.line: But as he came close, they couldn’t keep their pact. One took his bowl, one set out a seat, one brought water for his feet.
Then he taught them four truths. There is dukkha, the ache in life. It has a cause. It can end. And there is a path.

steps.q: Why isn’t the first truth a gloomy one?
o: It names what’s hard, so it can be treated
It promises that most of life is happy
It says pain is only in your mind
steps.why: It’s a diagnosis, not a verdict. Loss, change, things not fitting: everyone meets them. Naming it is step one.

steps.line: One friend, Kondanna, saw it first: whatever begins, also ends. “Kondanna has understood!” the Buddha said.

steps.q: Kondanna had met the Buddha long before. At the baby prince’s naming, what had young Kondanna predicted?
o: He would rule the whole world as king
He would surely leave home and awaken
He would be either a king or a sage
steps.why: Later tellings say eight wise men read the baby’s signs. Seven said king or sage; only Kondanna said he will awaken, and decades later he was first to understand him.

steps.q: Later teachers compared the four truths to a doctor’s visit. Match them.
steps.why: The cause is craving: a thirst for things to be other than they are. Its ending is called nirvana.

say: the four noble truths are the heart of the buddha’s first teaching. there is dukkha. it has a cause, craving. it can end. and there’s a path, with eight parts.
and the first truth isn’t a verdict. it doesn’t say life is bad, or that you’re doing it wrong. it says: this is hard, for everyone. then it gets to work.

steps.q: Kondanna saw that whatever begins, also ends. Why would that be good news for someone in pain?
o: Nothing lasts, so nothing really matters
Time will make you forget it in the end
Pain began, so pain can end too
steps.why: That’s the third truth: it can end. After that day he was called Añña Kondanna, Kondanna who knows.

today.say: today, when something’s hard, try the doctor’s first two steps. name it plainly: this is dukkha. then ask, gently: what am i clutching at?
options: naming it is the first truth. that’s real practice.
What if I can’t find the cause?
that’s okay. the first step already helps. it’s not just you.

sources: Vinaya, Mahavagga I.6: the journey to the deer park at Isipatana near Benares; the five monks’ agreement not to rise or greet him; one takes his bowl and robe, one prepares a seat, one sets out water for his feet
Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, Samyutta Nikaya 56.11: the four noble truths; Kondanna’s vision “whatever is subject to arising is subject to cessation”; “Kondanna has understood,” hence Añña Kondanna
Visuddhimagga XVI: the truths compared to a disease, its cause, its cure and the medicine
